say.text: Picture the right ventricle in TOF. It has two ways out: the RVOT, and a **large VSD** into the overriding aorta.

say.text: Blood leaves by the easier exit. In classic TOF one exit is a large VSD, the other is the RVOT.

say.text: Same idea, new angle. The VSD stays large. Only the RVOT tightens.

say.text: Yes. With significant RVOT obstruction, most of the blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the pulmonary bed.
That bypass is why a chest X-ray can show decreased pulmonary vascular markings (**pulmonary oligaemia**).

say.text: Which comparison decides whether a TOF patient is cyanotic?

choices.label: Resistance across the RVOT versus systemic vascular resistance
VSD diameter versus aortic diameter

say.text: Yes. If the resistance across the RVOT is less than the systemic vascular resistance, the patient is minimally cyanotic or acyanotic.
Tighten the RVOT and the balance tips: most of the blood shunts toward the aorta, bypassing the lungs.
